analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans buy up to a 90-day supply of prescription drugs directly from approved Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 15 cosponsors from both parties but never got a committee markup or a House vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA to write rules, within 180 days, allowing individuals to import prescription drugs they bought from certified Canadian pharmacies. A drug would qualify if it was dispensed by a licensed Canadian pharmacist, filled with a valid U.S. prescription, bought for personal use in a 90-day supply or less, and chemically identical to an FDA-approved drug. The FDA would have published a list of approved Canadian pharmacies that meet safety and quality standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. cash prices for prescription drugs, especially the uninsured and people with high deductibles, who could buy the same medication from a certified Canadian pharmacy at Canadian prices, which are often far lower.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans who pay high drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The FDA would have to issue regulations within 180 days of enactment permitting individuals to import qualifying prescription drugs from Canada for personal use.

Qualifying drugs must be purchased from an approved Canadian pharmacy, dispensed by a pharmacist licensed in Canada, filled with a valid U.S. prescription, limited to a 90-day personal supply, and identical in active ingredients, dosage form, and strength to an FDA-approved drug.

The FDA must certify Canadian pharmacies that meet standards — at least five years in operation, compliance with Canadian provincial pharmacy rules, quality assurance and blind testing programs, and accountability for violations — and publish a public list of approved pharmacies with their website addresses.

The bill excludes controlled substances, biological products, infused and intravenous drugs, refrigerated drugs, and other categories where safety risks are highest, leaving a narrower but safer set of importable drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose U.S. prices rely on a market closed to cheaper Canadian sales of the identical medicines; they would lose some U.S. sales to importation.

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes biological products, refrigerated drugs, and several other categories, which leaves out many of the newest and most expensive medicines, including most biologic drugs.

It relies on individual purchases of 90-day supplies rather than a system-wide price change, so savings depend on each person knowing about and using the program, and it does nothing to lower prices for people whose insurance covers the drug at the U.S. price.

Opponents of drug importation have long argued that personal importation is harder for the FDA to police for safety than domestic distribution; the bill's pharmacy certification and testing requirements are a response to that concern, but they do not eliminate it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people paying cash prices — the uninsured and the underinsured — the bill offered a concrete, safe-enough escape hatch from U.S. drug prices, with the safety exclusions and pharmacy certification designed to limit risk. Its honest limitation is scope: it would help individual buyers rather than lowering drug prices across the system, and its exclusions keep many of the priciest drugs out of reach. On balance a real benefit for those who need it most, with modest costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2019 and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chellie Pingree introduced the bill on January 10, 2019, joined by Rep. Jaime Herrera Beutler as an original cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and referred it to the Health Subcommittee on January 25, 2019.
The bill attracted 15 cosponsors, including 12 House Democrats and 3 House Republicans.
No further action was taken — no subcommittee or full committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: the U.S. market for their drugs remained closed to lower-priced Canadian imports, and the pricing status quo continued for another two years.

for.name: Chellie Pingree
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to allow personal drug importation from approved Canadian pharmacies.

for.name: Jaime Herrera Beutler
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as the lead Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a subcommittee or committee vote; it sat in committee for two years and expired.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry has long campaigned against prescription drug importation from Canada, arguing it undermines U.S. drug safety and their ability to fund research.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship split across party lines — 12 of 15 cosponsors were Democrats and 3 were Republicans — but the House leadership of either party never brought it to a vote.

industries.note: Importation would open the U.S. market to the same drugs sold at lower Canadian prices, cutting into U.S. sales. The industry's interest in keeping importation banned runs directly against consumers paying U.S. prices.

The bill would make certified Canadian pharmacies the permanent, FDA-approved channel for Americans to buy lower-priced drugs, with the FDA publishing their list. They gain customers; consumers gain lower prices.
